questions.question: Why does caching dramatically improve application performance?
options: It compresses data to reduce transfer time
It stores frequently accessed data in fast memory, avoiding slow database queries
It reduces the number of servers needed
It encrypts data for faster processing
questions.explanation: Caches store data in memory (RAM), which is orders of magnitude faster than disk-based database queries. Serving from cache avoids the expensive round-trip to the database.

questions.question: A cache hit occurs when:
options: The requested data is not found in the cache
The cache is full and an entry must be evicted
The requested data is found in the cache and returned directly
The cache server crashes
questions.explanation: A cache hit means the data the client requested is already stored in the cache, so it can be returned immediately without querying the database.

questions.question: TTL (Time to Live) on a cache entry determines:
options: How fast the cache responds to queries
How long the entry stays in cache before automatically expiring
The maximum size of the cached value
How many times the entry can be read
questions.explanation: TTL sets a countdown timer on each cache entry. Once expired, the entry is removed (or marked stale), forcing the next request to fetch fresh data from the source.

questions.question: LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction removes:
options: The newest entry in the cache
The entry that was accessed least recently when the cache is full
Random entries to make space
The largest entry by size
questions.explanation: When the cache is full and a new entry needs space, LRU evicts the entry that hasn't been accessed for the longest time, assuming recently used data is more likely to be needed again.

questions.question: In the cache-aside pattern, who is responsible for populating the cache?
options: The database automatically pushes data to the cache
The application code checks the cache, and on a miss, queries the DB and writes the result to cache
The cache fetches data from the database on its own
A separate background job populates the cache periodically
questions.explanation: In cache-aside (lazy loading), the application owns the caching logic: check cache first, on miss query the database, then store the result in cache for future requests.

questions.question: Write-through caching ensures:
options: Data is only written to the cache, never the database
Every write updates both the cache and the database, keeping them in sync
Writes bypass the cache entirely
The cache is cleared on every write
questions.explanation: Write-through writes data to both the cache and the database on every write operation. The cache always has fresh data, but write latency increases since two stores must complete.

questions.question: A cache stampede (thundering herd) happens when:
options: The cache is never used
A popular cache entry expires and many concurrent requests all miss and flood the database simultaneously
Too much data is stored in the cache
The cache server runs out of memory gracefully
questions.explanation: When a hot cache key expires, all concurrent requests see a miss at the same time and hit the database. This sudden load spike can overwhelm the database. Solutions include locking, staggered TTLs, or background refresh.

questions.question: Redis is commonly used as a cache because:
options: It stores data on disk for durability
It's an in-memory data store with sub-millisecond response times and rich data structures
It replaces the need for a database entirely
It only supports string data
questions.explanation: Redis keeps data in RAM for extremely fast access, supports diverse data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets), and offers features like TTL, pub/sub, and persistence options.

questions.question: LFU (Least Frequently Used) eviction differs from LRU in that LFU removes entries based on:
options: How recently they were accessed
How many times they have been accessed (lowest count gets evicted)
Their size in memory
Their creation timestamp
questions.explanation: LFU tracks access frequency and evicts the entry with the fewest total accesses. LRU evicts based on recency. LFU is better for workloads where some keys are consistently popular over long periods.

questions.question: Cache invalidation is considered hard because:
options: Caches can only store small amounts of data
Ensuring all cached copies are updated or removed when the source data changes across distributed systems is error-prone
TTL always solves the problem perfectly
Modern caches don't support invalidation
questions.explanation: In distributed systems with multiple cache layers and replicas, knowing exactly when and where to invalidate stale data is notoriously difficult. Stale reads, race conditions, and partial updates make this one of computing's hardest problems.
